chief_complaints.text: My lower back hurts and the pain shoots down my leg
My leg feels numb and tingly

hpi.onset: Usually gradual over days to weeks, sometimes sudden after lifting or bending
hpi.duration: Days to weeks at presentation; often improves within 4–6 weeks
hpi.progression: Starts as low back pain, then radiates down the buttock and leg; may worsen with activity before gradually improving
hpi.location: Lower back, buttock, and posterior or lateral thigh, radiating down the leg
hpi.radiation: Down the back of the thigh and leg, often to the calf, foot, or toes; usually one side only
hpi.quality: Sharp, shooting, burning, or electric shock-like
hpi.timing: Intermittent or constant; often worse with activity and at night

associated_symptoms.text: Numbness or tingling in the leg or foot
Weakness in the leg or foot
Muscle spasms in the back or leg
Feeling of heaviness in the leg

pertinent_negatives: Loss of bladder or bowel control
Numbness in the groin or inner thighs (saddle anesthesia)
Pain that is worse at rest or at night and relieved by sitting

negatives: Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour

positives.text: Numbness or tingling in the leg or foot

negatives: Loss of bowel or bladder control

atypical.how_it_differs: More likely due to spinal stenosis than a disc herniation; pain is often bilateral, worse with walking and standing, and relieved by sitting or bending forward. Classic unilateral radiating pain may be absent.
Leg pain may be from pelvic girdle relaxation or the weight of the uterus pressing on the sciatic nerve; symptoms are often bilateral and fluctuate with position.
Underlying diabetic peripheral neuropathy can cause burning or numbness in the feet that is not radicular; symptoms may be bilateral and length-dependent.
Increased mechanical load on the lumbar spine can cause more diffuse low back pain with less clear radicular features; exam may be limited by body habitus.

general.mild: Comfortable at rest, moves without guarding, no distress
general.moderate: Antalgic posture, shifts weight off the affected leg, winces when rising from a chair
general.severe: Markedly antalgic, stands with a lateral lean or forward stoop, reluctant to bend or sit
general.critical: Distressed, unable to bear weight, may have saddle anesthesia or leg weakness; requires urgent evaluation

findings.maneuver: With the patient supine, lift the affected leg by the heel with the knee extended
findings.finding: Reproduction of radiating pain down the leg at 30–70 degrees of hip flexion

findings.maneuver: Lift the unaffected leg with the knee extended
findings.finding: Radiating pain in the affected leg

findings.maneuver: Dorsiflex the ankle while the leg is raised (or lower the leg until pain resolves, then dorsiflex)
findings.finding: Recurrence of radiating leg pain with ankle dorsiflexion

findings.maneuver: Test light touch and pinprick in the L4, L5 and S1 dermatomes bilaterally
findings.finding: Decreased sensation in a dermatomal distribution (L5 or S1 most often)
Weakness of foot dorsiflexion or great toe extension
Weakness of ankle plantarflexion or difficulty with heel raises

findings.maneuver: Tap the Achilles tendon with a reflex hammer
Tap the patellar tendon with a reflex hammer
Palpate the lumbar paraspinal muscles and spinous processes
Ask the patient to bend forward at the waist
findings.finding: Limited lumbar flexion due to pain or muscle spasm

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient walking and on heel and toe walking
findings.finding: Normal gait without foot drop or wide-based unsteadiness

findings.maneuver: Test sensation in the perineal and saddle area
Perform a digital rectal exam when cauda equina syndrome is suspected
findings.finding: Normal anal sphincter tone and no saddle anesthesia

findings.maneuver: Perform the femoral stretch test (prone, flex the knee and extend the hip)
findings.finding: No anterior thigh pain, arguing against upper lumbar radiculopathy

findings.maneuver: Palpate the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses
findings.finding: Palpable symmetric pulses, arguing against vascular claudication

findings.maneuver: Test hip internal and external rotation and perform FABER test
findings.finding: No hip pain or restriction, arguing against hip arthritis or bursitis

decision_points: Check for red flags (saddle anesthesia, bowel or bladder dysfunction, progressive weakness, fever, cancer history, trauma) before deciding on urgent imaging
Urgent MRI and surgical consultation for suspected cauda equina syndrome or progressive motor deficit
Pregnancy test before imaging or medication in anyone who could be pregnant
Most patients without red flags can be managed conservatively for 4–6 weeks before imaging

differential.name: Cauda equina syndrome
differential.why_considered: Lumbar disc herniation is the most common cause of sciatica and can compress the cauda equina, producing bilateral leg pain with bladder, bowel and saddle symptoms.
differential.trigger: Saddle anesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, fecal incontinence, or rapidly progressive bilateral leg weakness

history: Urinary retention or overflow incontinence
Loss of bowel control
Numbness in the groin, perineum or inner thighs
Bilateral or rapidly progressive leg weakness
Severe low back pain with sudden onset
exam: Reduced or absent perineal and saddle sensation
Reduced anal sphincter tone on digital rectal exam
Bilateral leg weakness or asymmetric severe deficits
Absent ankle reflexes bilaterally
labs: No specific blood test confirms it; urinalysis and post-void residual help assess retention
imaging: Urgent MRI showing a large central disc herniation or mass compressing multiple nerve roots of the cauda equina
Loss of normal nerve root definition and crowding of the thecal sac

differential.name: Lumbar spinal stenosis
differential.why_considered: Narrowing of the spinal canal compresses nerve roots and causes radiating leg pain, especially in older adults.

history: Older age, typically over 60
Bilateral or alternating leg pain and heaviness
Pain worse with walking and standing, relieved by sitting or bending forward
Symptoms improve when leaning on a shopping cart
exam: Symptoms provoked by lumbar extension
Relatively preserved straight leg raise
Often normal or mildly reduced reflexes
Wide-based gait or unsteadiness in advanced cases
imaging: MRI or CT showing central canal or foraminal narrowing, ligamentum flavum hypertrophy and facet arthropathy

differential.name: Vascular claudication
differential.why_considered: Exertional leg pain that limits walking can be mistaken for neurogenic claudication from sciatica.

history: Cramping calf or thigh pain brought on by walking a predictable distance
Relieved within minutes of standing still, not by sitting or bending forward
History of smoking, diabetes, hypertension or hyperlipidemia
No back pain
exam: Diminished or absent dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses
Cool, shiny, hairless skin with dependent rubor
Femoral bruit
Symptoms not reproduced by straight leg raise
imaging: Arterial duplex or CT angiography showing stenosis or occlusion

differential.name: Hip osteoarthritis
differential.why_considered: Pain referred from the hip can radiate to the buttock, groin and thigh and be confused with sciatica.

history: Pain in the groin and anterior thigh rather than below the knee
Worse with weight bearing and at the end of the day
Stiffness after inactivity
No numbness or tingling
exam: Reduced and painful hip internal and external rotation
Positive FABER test
No dermatomal sensory loss
Straight leg raise does not reproduce radiating leg pain
imaging: Hip x-ray showing joint space narrowing, osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis

differential.name: Piriformis syndrome
differential.why_considered: The sciatic nerve can be compressed by the piriformis muscle, causing buttock and posterior thigh pain that mimics radiculopathy.

history: Pain centered in the buttock, worse with sitting or climbing stairs
No back pain
Often after prolonged sitting or a fall on the buttock
exam: Tenderness over the piriformis and greater sciatic notch
Pain reproduced by internal rotation and adduction of the flexed hip (FAIR test)
Normal neurologic exam including reflexes and dermatomal sensation
Straight leg raise may be positive but no dermatomal deficit
imaging: MRI of the lumbar spine is normal
MRI of the pelvis may show piriformis enlargement or sciatic nerve signal change

differential.name: Herpes zoster (shingles)
differential.why_considered: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in a lumbar dermatome causes burning, shooting pain in a radicular pattern.

history: Burning or lancinating pain preceding a rash by days
Pain confined to a single dermatome
No relation to activity or position
May have had chickenpox or be immunocompromised
exam: Vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution
Allodynia and hyperesthesia in the affected dermatome
No weakness or reflex changes unless motor involvement
labs: Varicella-zoster virus PCR from vesicle fluid if diagnosis is uncertain

differential.name: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy
differential.why_considered: Diabetes can cause burning, tingling and numbness in the legs that may be mistaken for radicular pain.

history: Long-standing diabetes
Symptoms begin in the toes and feet and ascend symmetrically
No back pain
No positional or activity-related pattern
exam: Stocking-distribution sensory loss
Reduced vibration and pinprick sensation in the feet
Absent ankle reflexes bilaterally
Normal straight leg raise
labs: Electromyography and nerve conduction studies showing a symmetric, length-dependent sensorimotor polyneuropathy

severity.mild: Intermittent shooting leg pain with no or minimal functional limitation; normal strength, reflexes and sensation; able to work and perform activities of daily living.
severity.moderate: Constant or frequent leg pain limiting walking and sitting tolerance; mild dermatomal sensory loss or subjective weakness; positive straight leg raise; requires regular analgesics.
severity.severe: Disabling pain with marked antalgic posture; objective weakness in a myotome, reduced reflex, or significant functional impairment; unable to work or walk more than a short distance.
severity.critical: Cauda equina syndrome or rapidly progressive motor deficit: saddle anesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, fecal incontinence, or bilateral severe leg weakness requiring emergency decompression.

red_flags.finding: Saddle anesthesia or numbness in the groin and inner thighs
red_flags.meaning: Suggests cauda equina syndrome; requires emergency MRI and surgical consultation

red_flags.finding: Urinary retention, overflow incontinence or loss of bowel control
red_flags.meaning: Cauda equina syndrome until proven otherwise; emergency evaluation

red_flags.finding: Rapidly progressive or severe bilateral leg weakness
red_flags.meaning: Significant nerve root or cord compression; urgent imaging and neurosurgical referral

red_flags.finding: Fever, chills or night sweats with back pain
red_flags.meaning: Possible spinal infection such as discitis, osteomyelitis or epidural abscess

red_flags.finding: History of cancer with new back and leg pain, or pain worse at rest and at night
red_flags.meaning: Possible metastatic spinal disease or pathologic fracture

red_flags.finding: Significant trauma or minor trauma in an osteoporotic patient
red_flags.meaning: Possible vertebral fracture causing nerve root compression

red_flags.finding: Unexplained weight loss or constitutional symptoms
red_flags.meaning: Concern for malignancy or systemic infection

complications.name: Persistent radicular pain and functional limitation
Motor weakness and foot drop
clues: Weakness of ankle dorsiflexion or great toe extension

complications.name: Cauda equina syndrome
clues: Large central disc herniation on MRI

special_populations.differences: More likely due to lumbar spinal stenosis than a disc herniation; symptoms are often bilateral, worse with walking and standing, and relieved by sitting or bending forward. Osteoporosis increases the risk of vertebral fracture, and imaging should include assessment for fracture and malignancy.

Leg pain may arise from pelvic girdle relaxation or the gravid uterus pressing on the sciatic nerve; symptoms are often bilateral and fluctuate with position. MRI without contrast can be used when needed, and management avoids medications that are unsafe in pregnancy.

Underlying diabetic peripheral neuropathy can cause burning or numbness in the feet that is not radicular; symptoms may be bilateral and length-dependent. Glycemic control and foot care are important, and electromyography helps distinguish the two.

Increased mechanical load on the lumbar spine can cause more diffuse low back pain with less clear radicular features; exam may be limited by body habitus. Weight reduction is part of long-term management.

key_questions.question: Where does the pain go, and how far down the leg does it reach?
key_questions.looking_for: Pain radiating from the lower back or buttock down the posterior or lateral thigh, often past the knee to the calf, foot or toes, usually one side only

key_questions.question: What does the pain feel like?
key_questions.looking_for: Sharp, shooting, burning or electric shock-like quality rather than a dull ache

key_questions.question: What makes the pain worse or better?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse with sitting, bending, lifting, coughing or straining; relieved by lying down or changing position

key_questions.question: When and how did it start?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over days to weeks, or sudden after lifting or bending; duration helps decide on imaging

key_questions.question: Do you have numbness, tingling or weakness in the leg or foot?
key_questions.looking_for: Numbness or tingling in a dermatomal pattern, or weakness such as tripping or foot drop

key_questions.question: Have you had any trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, or numbness in the groin or inner thighs?
key_questions.looking_for: Urinary retention or incontinence, fecal incontinence, or saddle anesthesia suggesting cauda equina syndrome

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, chills, night sweats or unexplained weight loss?
key_questions.looking_for: Constitutional symptoms raising concern for spinal infection or malignancy

key_questions.question: Have you ever been diagnosed with cancer?
key_questions.looking_for: History of cancer, which raises concern for metastatic spinal disease

key_questions.question: Was there any recent trauma or fall?
key_questions.looking_for: Significant trauma or minor trauma in an osteoporotic patient suggesting vertebral fracture

key_questions.question: What do you do for work, and does it involve heavy lifting or long periods of sitting or driving?
key_questions.looking_for: Occupational risk factors such as heavy lifting, repetitive bending or prolonged sitting

key_questions.question: Does the pain in your leg come on after walking a certain distance and go away when you stop and stand still?
key_questions.looking_for: Predictable exertional pain relieved by standing still, suggesting vascular claudication rather than radiculopathy

key_questions.question: Is the pain worse at rest or at night, and is it relieved by sitting?
key_questions.looking_for: Pain worse at rest or at night raises concern for infection or malignancy

reasoning_points: Pain radiates from the lower back or buttock down the posterior or lateral leg in a dermatomal pattern, usually unilateral
Sharp, shooting or burning quality worsened by sitting, bending, lifting, coughing or straining and relieved by lying down
Associated numbness, tingling or weakness in the leg or foot
Straight leg raise reproduces radiating leg pain, and dermatomal sensory loss, weakness or a reduced reflex supports nerve root involvement
Red flags for cauda equina syndrome, infection, malignancy or fracture are absent
Vascular claudication, hip arthritis, piriformis syndrome and diabetic peripheral neuropathy are considered and excluded
Imaging is reserved for red flags, progressive deficits or symptoms persisting beyond 4 to 6 weeks of conservative care

easy: Working-age adult with classic unilateral shooting pain from the back down the leg past the knee
Pain worse with sitting, coughing or straining and relieved by lying down
Positive straight leg raise reproducing the radiating pain
Dermatomal sensory loss or a reduced reflex matching the affected nerve root
medium: Older adult with bilateral leg pain worse with walking and standing, relieved by sitting or bending forward, suggesting spinal stenosis
Pain radiating to the groin or anterior thigh rather than below the knee, suggesting hip pathology
Buttock-centered pain with normal neurologic exam, suggesting piriformis syndrome
Long-standing diabetes with symmetric burning feet, suggesting diabetic peripheral neuropathy
hard: Older adult with mild back and leg pain and a normal neurologic exam
Pregnant patient with bilateral fluctuating leg pain from pelvic girdle relaxation or the gravid uterus
Patient with exertional calf cramping and diminished pedal pulses, suggesting vascular claudication
Patient presenting with saddle anesthesia, urinary retention or bilateral leg weakness from cauda equina syndrome
Patient with fever, weight loss or cancer history and pain worse at rest, suggesting infection or malignancy
